### Problem: Same Differences {#sec-hash-p2-a}

::: {.p-statement}
For each test case, given an array $a$ of $n$ integers **indexed from 1** ($1 \le n \le 2\cdot10^5$, $1 \le a_i \le n$; the sum of $n$ over test cases is at most $2\cdot10^5$), count pairs $(i, j)$ with $i < j$ and $a_j - a_i = j - i$. Up to $10^4$ test cases.

Source: [CF 1520D · Same Differences](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1520/D){.solved rating="1200"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Rearrange $a_j - a_i = j - i$ into $a_i - i = a_j - j$: the pair condition is *equality of a value you can compute per index*. Once you see the key, the answer is pure grouping — a group of $c$ equal keys contributes $\binom{c}{2}$ pairs (@sec-hash-keys).
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Brute force.** Test all $\binom{n}{2}$ index pairs directly: $O(n^2)$ per test, dead on arrival at $n = 2\cdot10^5$.
2. **Group by the key.** One pass computes $a_i - i$ for every position and counts collisions in a hash map; a second, tiny pass sums $c(c-1)/2$ over the groups. $O(n)$.

**Invariant.** After processing positions $1..i$, `cnt[k]` equals the number of those positions with $a_j - j = k$.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Test every index pair

::: {.form-next}
Two loops and the equation straight from the statement. $O(n^2)$ per test — $4\cdot10^{10}$ at $n = 2\cdot10^5$, the clearest possible signal that the equation wants to be *rearranged into a key*.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def same_diffs_brute(a):
    n = len(a)
    return sum(1 for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n)
               if (a[j] - a[i]) == (j - i))     # 1-based shift cancels
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

long long sameDiffsBrute(const vector<int>& a) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    long long pairs = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; ++j)
            if (a[j] - a[i] == j - i) ++pairs;
    return pairs;
}
```
:::

#### Group by a[i] - i, count within groups

::: {.form-next}
The equation rearranges to $a_i - i = a_j - j$, so matching positions share a **key**, and keys can be counted in one pass. Positions with equal keys form groups of size $c$; every pair inside a group works, so add $\binom{c}{2}$. Keys are negative sometimes — hash-map territory, not a frequency array (@sec-hash-keys).
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("samediff", "key")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-same-differences
def same_differences(a: list[int]) -> int:
    cnt = Counter(x - i for i, x in enumerate(a, start=1))
    return sum(c * (c - 1) // 2 for c in cnt.values())


for _ in range(800):
    a = [random.randint(1, 12) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 16))]
    assert same_differences(a) == same_diffs_brute(a)

assert same_differences([3, 5, 1, 4, 6, 6]) == 1     # all four CF samples,
assert same_differences([1, 2, 3]) == 3              # verified against the
assert same_differences([1, 3, 3, 4]) == 3           # problem's own outputs
assert same_differences([1, 6, 3, 4, 5, 6]) == 10    # (board sample is test 3)
assert same_differences([7]) == 0
print("same_differences OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

void solve() {
    int n; cin >> n;
    unordered_map<long long, long long> cnt;   // key -> group size so far
    long long ans = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
        long long x; cin >> x;
        ans += cnt[x - i];         // every earlier equal key pairs with me
        ++cnt[x - i];              // ... then I join the group
    }
    cout << ans << '\n';
}

int main() { ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);
    int t; cin >> t; while (t--) solve(); }
```
:::
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Test every index pair** is $O(n^2)$ per test — impossible at these constraints. **Group by a[i] - i, count within groups** is $O(n)$ expected per test, $O(n)$ space; it also adds each pair the moment it is completed (`ans += cnt[key]`), so no second pass over the map is even needed — the C++ listing does exactly that. Under contest pressure with `long long` keys, armour the hash or use `map` for guaranteed $O(n\log n)$ (@sec-hash-anti).
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- 1-based or 0-based indices: either works, as long as every key uses the same convention — switching from $i$ to $i - 1$ adds $1$ to every key, and equal keys stay equal.
- All keys distinct: answer $0$. All keys equal (e.g. $a = [1,2,3]$): $\binom{n}{2}$ — fits in `long long` at $n = 2\cdot10^5$ ($\approx 2\cdot10^{10}$), an `int` would wrap (@sec-arr-cost).
- $1 \le a_i \le n$ bounds the keys to $[1 - n, n - 1]$, so a frequency array with offset $n$ also works and cannot be attacked; the hash map works without needing the bound.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [LC 1512 · Number of Good Pairs](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-good-pairs/){difficulty="Easy"} — $\binom{c}{2}$ with the value itself as the key; the smallest instance of this pattern.
- [LC 2364 · Count Number of Bad Pairs](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-number-of-bad-pairs/){difficulty="Medium"} — the same key $a_i - i$; count the good pairs and subtract them from $\binom{n}{2}$.
:::
